data.title: Semantic Versioning
data.tagline: A versioning rule that uses major, minor, and patch to express a public API compatibility promise
data.learningOutcome: When a project uses SemVer, you can read the compatibility promise in X.Y.Z and know to check project documentation and actual changes too.
data.description: SemVer uses X.Y.Z to express a promise about public API compatibility: for stable versions, patch means a compatible fix, minor means a compatible addition, and major means an incompatible change. A version is the author’s API contract, not an application upgrade risk score; 0.y.z versions have not promised a stable API.

learning.assumes: You have seen version numbers on dependencies, or hit errors after an upgrade.
learning.outcome: When a project uses SemVer, you can read the compatibility promise in X.Y.Z and know to check project documentation and actual changes too.

distinctions.label: Date versioning
distinctions.explanation: Date versions like 2026.09 only mark release time; semantic versioning's three segments each express a change's impact.

distinctions.label: Build number
distinctions.explanation: A build number only counts builds and says nothing about compatibility; semantic versioning exists to announce compatibility.

explanation.title: Patch: usually a fix
explanation.text: For a stable public API, a patch change promises a compatible fix. Check the project's release notes and run its acceptance checks after upgrading.

explanation.title: Minor: usually new features
explanation.text: For a stable public API, a minor release promises compatible additions; check whether the new features affect you.

explanation.title: Major: possibly incompatible
explanation.text: For a stable public API, a major release signals incompatible changes; read the release notes before upgrading and verify your project flows afterward.

data.boundary: In npm, ^1.2.3 allows minor and patch updates within major version 1, not 2.0.0; ~1.2.3 allows patch updates within 1.2. The ^ and ~ symbols are npm range syntax, not part of SemVer. Other package managers may differ, so check their documentation.

lessonPractice.title: The example library sample-lib is at ^1.2.3, and AI suggests changing it to 2.0.0 because newer is better. What is the more careful approach?

options.label: Check the 2.0.0 release notes for breaking changes and assess the impact before upgrading
options.feedback: Correct. A major version change can include breaking changes; the release notes list them and are required reading before upgrading.

options.label: Always use the newest version because newer is always better
options.feedback: A newer number does not mean compatible; a major bump can invalidate existing code.

options.label: Never upgrade and lock every dependency at its lowest version
options.feedback: Never upgrading accumulates security and compatibility problems; upgrade deliberately based on release notes.

data.agentPrompt: The example library sample-lib is at ^1.2.3. First read the 2.0.0 release notes and list the changes that affect this project, then decide whether to upgrade. If you upgrade, check every page for errors afterward and do not upgrade other dependencies along the way.
